provenance: Opus 5.5 subscription CLI draft with host review/repairs, source restrictions and execution verification.

draft_notes.explanation: The palette fixes the colour roles as constants. Background is palette[7], blobs are palette[4], the bar is palette[5] and the gun cell is palette[9]. The emitted program works directly in the visible grid coordinates. It finds the gun cell and the bar cell that is orthogonally adjacent to it, which is the bar's centre. The step from the gun to that centre gives the firing direction. Any D4 rotation or reflection simply turns this into another of the four axis directions, so nothing needs to be un-transformed. The program then walks the ray from the gun cell to the edge of the grid. Whenever the ray meets a blob-coloured cell, it flood-fills that cell's whole 4-connected blob to background. Blobs that only touch the ray diagonally, or only touch the bar, are left alone. This matches the constructor, which erases every 4-connected yellow component that intersects the ray from the 9 onward. If no bar cell is adjacent to the gun, the program falls back to the sign of the vector from the gun to the mean bar position, kept on one axis.
draft_notes.limitations: The program assumes the palette is injective and that each grid contains exactly one gun cell and one 3-cell bar, as the constructor guarantees. If there were several gun cells, only the first in reading order would be used. Demonstrations are not needed and are ignored, because the colour roles come from the palette. The four approved fixtures follow this rule uniformly; I found no contradictions. I have not run any tests.
